message.content: Lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) belong to two very different mammalian orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively. Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). This ancestor was a small, shrew‑like mammal that lived roughly 100–110 million years ago during the early Paleocene, after the mass extinction that wiped out the non‑avian dinosaurs. From that point onward, the lineages that would become carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates diverged, eventually giving rise to the diverse groups we see today.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, or maybe earlier. But we can give a more precise answer: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). That ancestor lived around 100 million years ago. So answer: the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, likely a small mammal-like creature from the Paleocene. Provide details.
